new_statements.quote: 9. MUSIKALISCHE TÖNE. Der musikalische Ton ist in der Sprache vorhanden; in welchem Ausmasse er von Bedeutung ist, kann ich nicht sagen. Die geringen mir zur Verfügung stehenden Beispiele zeigen einen tiefen, einen hohen und einen fallenden Ton: ì Frau, í du, tók warum? tòk zehn, wâdney ich bewerbe mich. 10. STARKTON. Der in den einzelnen Wörtern angegebene Akut ( ' ) bezeichnet den Starkton; er ist mit dem musikalischen Ton nicht zu verwechseln, da ich diesen mit Akut und Gravis ausser in den oben § 9 angegebenen Beispielen nirgends bezeichnet habe.
new_statements.translation: 9. MUSICAL TONES. Musical tone is present in the language; to what extent it is significant I cannot say. The few examples at my disposal show a low, a high and a falling tone: ì 'woman', í 'you', tók 'why?', tòk 'ten', wâdney 'I court'. 10. STRESS (Starkton). The acute ( ' ) given on the individual words marks the (dynamic) stress; it is not to be confused with the musical tone, since I have not marked the latter with acute and grave anywhere except in the examples given in § 9 above.
new_statements.citation: Lukas, Johannes. 1933. Beiträge zur Kenntnis der Sprachen von Wadái (Mararét, Mába). Journal de la Société des Africanistes 3(1): 25-55. DOI 10.3406/jafr.1933.1543
new_statements.locator: § 9 'Musikalische Töne' and § 10 'Starkton', pp. 30-31 (page images); cf. p. 44 fn. 1
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lukas states that Mararit has both pitch tone (low/high/falling, functional load undetermined) and a dynamic word stress, which he marks with an acute on every cited word; he gives no rule for its position. His marked forms place it on different syllables (initial: ókur 'dove', tárak 'leaf', kíňet 'tree'; final: kugút 'hen', kugudáň 'hens'; on the ending in verb forms like nògudéy 'I see'), and in the -ey verb class he notes that sometimes the stem and sometimes the ending is stressed, suggesting stem-stressed vs ending-stressed verb classes (p. 44 fn. 1). Position therefore reads as lexically/morphologically variable rather than fixed, but the source does not say so explicitly.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 44 fn. 1: 'es [gibt] allem Anschein nach auch im Mararét in dieser Verbenklasse einen Unterschied in der Betonung..., als das eine Mal der Stamm, das andere Mal die Endung betont ist' (stem- vs ending-stressed verbs, as in Kanuri); p. 51 note to text II.6: the form nèsènï appears 'in etwas anderer Betonung' as nésini in § 32 — stress placement varies between recordings of the same form.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: isolated words, noun and verb paradigms and six short texts elicited in Cairo (winter 1928-29) from a single speaker, Mohammed Raschíd, over about one month; Lukas explicitly hedges about the tone system. Variety = Mararit proper (speaker's name for the language: ebiri, i.e. Abiri/Ebiri).
new_statements.identity_note: Lukas's 'Mararét' is Mararit proper (his speaker called the language ebiri = Abiri/Ebiri, one of Glottolog's alternate names for mara1396); the Abu Sharib and Darnut dialects reported by Rilly (2010)/Edgar (1991) are not separately described in any opened source. Glottolog lists no child dialects for mara1396.

Die geringen mir zur Verfügung stehenden Beispiele zeigen einen tiefen, einen hohen und einen fallenden Ton: ì Frau, í du, tók warum? tòk zehn, wâdney ich bewerbe mich. 10. STARKTON. Der in den einzelnen Wörtern angegebene Akut ( ' ) bezeichnet den Starkton; er ist mit dem musikalischen Ton nicht zu verwechseln, da ich diesen mit Akut und Gravis ausser in den oben § 9 angegebenen Beispielen nirgends bezeichnet habe.
sources.locator: § 9 'Musikalische Töne' and § 10 'Starkton', pp. 30-31 (page images); cf. p. 44 fn. 1
sources.note: § 9 (p. 30): musical tone exists (low, high, falling), its functional load unknown; § 10 (pp. 30-31): the acute on each cited word marks the Starkton (dynamic stress), distinct from tone, which is marked only in the § 9 examples; no positional rule given; p. 44 fn. 1: in the -ey verb class stress falls sometimes on the stem, sometimes on the ending, suggesting stem- vs ending-stressed verb classes as in Kanuri. (The 'Akzent auf der zweiten/ersten Silbe' remarks on pp. 37, 39 concern the Maba footnote paradigms, not Mararit.)
